title: Polymorphism: one call, different code
intro: A variable of type Animal holds a Dog, then a Cat. Same call each time. What happens?

predict.question: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); Dog overrides speak() to print Woof. What prints?
options: Woof, because the real object is a Dog
A generic Animal sound, because a is an Animal
predict.reveal: Java looks at the real object on the heap, not the variable type. The object is a Dog, so Dog's speak() runs.

takeaway: The variable type decides what you can call; the real object decides which version of the method runs.

steps.say: Dog and Cat are both kinds of Animal, and each writes its own speak(). Let's see which one runs when we only hold an Animal variable.
The variable a has type Animal, but new Dog() builds a Dog on the heap. A parent-type variable may point at any child object.
steps.note: variable type: Animal, real object: Dog

steps.say: a.speak(): Java follows the arrow to the real object, finds a Dog, and runs Dog's version. It prints Woof.

cpu.doing: follow a to d1, run Dog.speak()

steps.say: Now a = new Cat(). Same variable, new arrow: a points at a Cat object. The Dog still sits on the heap for a moment.
The line a.speak() is word for word the same as before. But this time Java finds a Cat at the end of the arrow, so Meow.

cpu.doing: follow a to c1, run Cat.speak()

steps.say: Nothing points at the Dog any more, so it is garbage. The garbage collector can free it.
Catch: the variable type decides what you may CALL (a.speak() compiles), the real object decides WHICH code runs. This is decided while running.
steps.note: a.fetch() would not compile on an Animal

steps.say: So one call, a.speak(), gave two behaviours. That is polymorphism: many forms behind one method name.
